items.title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.original_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims get the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Read More Breaking Down Silos in Insurance by Rory Meleniclis Insurers can dismantle organizational silos by shifting from project-based work to product teams built around shared capabilities like underwriting and claims. Read More How AI Can Transform Submissions for Underwriting by Prathap Gokul Commercial insurers face a strategic challenge: identifying which submissions merit scarce underwriting attention, not just processing more faster. Read More Making AI Work in Commercial Submission Intake by Vital Soupel Insurers need a practical blueprint for where to apply AI first, how to move beyond pilots, and how to scale the technology responsibly. items.summary: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims get the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? items.title: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.original_title: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_title: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_description: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:16 Scammers increasingly impersonate insurers to steal identities and money during open enrollment. November 12, 2026 Image Last year, the Justice Department brought the largest healthcare fraud case in its history, which included charges that criminals stole the identities of more than 1 million Americans to submit $10.6 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims for urinary catheters. While Medicare blocked nearly all of it, private Medicare supplemental insurers paid out about $900 million. Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet crime in 2025, up 26% in one year, according to the FBI. Insurance fraud, including healthcare fraud, costs Americans more than $300 billion a year, and health insurance scams pick up during open enrollment, the FTC says. Seniors are the hardest-hit age group, losing $7.7 billion in 2025, up 59% in one year. In fact, Michigan officials warned on Oct. 12 of impostors claiming to be from Medicare to dupe older adults. As co-founder of Spokeo , a people search company, and former co-chair of the W3C Credentials Community Group , I have witnessed firsthand how scammers have grown increasingly sophisticated over the last 20 years. Insurance scams are evolving and costly We are seeing many insurance-related scams in 2026. Fraudsters are buying sponsored search ads with web addresses and logos that look very similar to HealthCare.gov and Medicare.gov . When Americans click on the link, they end up buying a plan that is not real insurance and also fork over their personal information, which can lead to identity theft. Even large health insurers are being duped, as the $900 million loss in the catheter case shows. The Coalition Against Insurance Fraud calls insurance fraud "the crime we all pay for," because it comes back to honest policyholders as higher premiums, which can hurt retention. In a September survey by BrandShield , 30% of U.S. adults said they would stop buying online from brands scammers had impersonated. For an insurer, that is a renewal lost to a scam it never ran. Here are three tips for insurers to help prevent insurance fraud Say what you will never do. Tell customers you will never ask for a one-time code or take payment by gift card, wire or crypto. Put the statement on the ID card, in the app, and on every renewal notice. Explain what numbers to trust and verify. Scammers can spoof caller ID so your company's name appears on a customer's phone. In every fraud alert, encourage customers to use the number on their card and check the identity of incoming callers with a reverse phone search . Report fake ads and websites and warn consumers. Search regularly for impostors using your name and report them to the FBI IC3 , the FTC , and the online platform where they live. Send alerts to customers in real time. Harrison Tang

items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. items.extracted_text: ILS seeks growth beyond property cat as investors explore new opportunities: PwC Insurance Summit - Artemis.bm ILS seeks growth beyond property cat as investors explore new opportunities: PwC Insurance Summit - Artemis.bm ILS seeks growth beyond property cat as investors explore new opportunities: PwC Insurance Summit 13th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard An ILS focused panel at PwC’s Insurance Summit in Bermuda this week underlined how the market is entering a new phase. After three decades of growth in property catastrophe, investors and market participants are looking toward specialty, casualty and cyber risks, and asking what infrastructure will be needed to make that expansion work. The panel was moderated by Sean Kelly, Partner, Insurance, PwC Bermuda. He was joined by insurance-linked securities experts, Chris Parry, Senior VP and Global Head of Capital Partners at RenaissanceRe Capital Partners Michael Millette, Co-Founder & Managing Partner at Hudson Structured Capital Management Ltd and Kathleen Faries, CEO at Artex Capital Solutions. Kicking off the discussion, Kelly asked the panelists to look back at how much the relationship between insurance and the capital markets has changed over the past 30 years. “Today we are definitely living in the catastrophe sector in a world where the capital markets capacity is important side by side with the traditional market,” said Millette. He estimated that capital markets provide about $140 billion of the roughly $500 billion in global catastrophe limits, with a particularly significant role in Florida and retrocession. But the opportunity discussed by the panel extends beyond catastrophe risk. Millette pointed to the growing participation of alternative asset managers in life insurance, as well as early capital markets involvement in casualty and cyber. The shift, he said, reflects a change in how the industry views its relationship with traditional insurers. “ The rhetoric of the late ’90s was a rhetoric of competition. You know, will these capital markets guys drive the traditional market out of business, or do they not know what they’re doing? A lot of back and forth, and the rhetoric today is of side-by-side. It’s a rhetoric of bulk capacity in the capital markets, underwriting in the insurance markets, that has become, in some ways, very functional and potentially very elegant,” Millette explained. That expansion is also changing the investor base, as Parry said the insurance-linked securities market has moved from attracting more opportunistic investors toward working with long-term pools of capital, including pension funds and sovereign wealth funds. Those investors, he said, are more inclined to take a “holistic view when it comes to partnerships.” “And I think that’s a very different conversation we’re having now with our investors than we would have done even pre the 2017/2018 soft market. So those conversations have evolved tremendously, and I think it allows you to think more long-term, obviously, but also just the more expansive nature of those conversations with the type of investors,” he added. For some ILS investors, the appeal remains diversification, with Millette emphasising that the value of non-correlation has risen as investors have seen traditional assets such as stocks and bonds move in the same direction. “25 years ago, pensions and endowments counted on stocks and bonds not to move the same way, such that they could get some buffer in their portfolio. 2022, we saw both stock and bond markets take a wallop at the same time. Lately, they’ve risen at the same time. Investors really crave diversification and non-correlation has gained in value, and that’s part of the reason,” Millette said. He continued: “It’s been a good story. It hasn’t been perfect, and it’s important that it hasn’t been perfect. But we had a messy period in the cat market from 2017 to 2022, we had a long spell of nasty weather and fierce wildfires, and investors came back quickly, and they did for all sorts of reasons. But they especially came back because the value of non-correlation is more important than it ever used to be for long-term investors.” However, the market’s evolution is not limited to risks that are uncorrelated with financial markets. Parry underlined that investors are increasingly considering areas such as credit, cyber and specialty, where correlation may be higher, alongside catastrophe exposure. The next stage of the market’s evolution may depend less on attracting capital than on building the efficient structures to deploy it, as Faries argues that expanding into more complex risks requires the right expertise, continued investor education and infrastructure that can support efficient execution. “If we’re going to go beyond property cat, which we are, I think we do need different pools of capital that have different risk appetites, different liquidity perspectives and different duration appetites. So it’s going to be super important that we move beyond what maybe was the type of ILS investor that we’ve had in the past, and that is happening,” Faries said. “I think there’s a lot of examples of that. If you think about Bermuda as maybe being over the last 30 years that window into accessing cat risk. Now we have obviously London with London Bridge 2 where now we’ve got a window into specialty risk, which is a very different investment with a lot more complexity.” “So there’s a lot more things that we have to think about again. But we do need different capital to be able to bring capital to those types of risks,” she continued. “ So I think it’s a super interesting time. But again, what made London Bridge 2 successful, in my view is they were thinking about what is the infrastructure that we need that’s going to maintain good trust, good execution, and make it efficient. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: Cortina: Just a soft market trend, or clearing the floor for reinsurance's next act? - Artemis.bm Cortina: Just a soft market trend, or clearing the floor for reinsurance's next act? - Artemis.bm Cortina: Just a soft market trend, or clearing the floor for reinsurance’s next act? 13th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Cortina has raised a lot of questions in the market, as to whether the recently launched Aon structured and Blackstone backed reinsurance facility at Lloyd’s is simply the latest iteration of a soft market trend and evolution of following, tracker style capacity, or something more portending of future market developments. There’s a fascinating metaphor buried in the name Cortina, one that we completely missed. Kudos to the analyst team at J.P. Morgan led by Kamran Hossain for spotting it, bringing it to our attention in their latest report and providing the inspiration. A Cortina is a specific tango-related phrase, a brief musical interlude within the Argentine milonga (a social tango event), used to signal the end of one dance, the clearing of the floor for a new set of dancers, and it often signals a structural change to the rhythm that has been played. Apply that to reinsurance and the Lloyd’s market and Cortina becomes a signal of something potentially more meaningful and perhaps ominous, than just an extension of Aon’s Client Treaty with a single backer. The use of lead-follow capacity strategies at Lloyd’s is not new, in fact the market has been dancing to the same rhythm for decades. This has relied on a deep network of pure-play reinsurers, falling into line behind a lead underwriter. While the recent launch of Cortina syndicate 1956 gave little away in terms of the thinking behind the structure or strategy, aside from it being a way for Blackstone ( third-party capital ) to secure preferential access to a large amount of reinsurance business from Lloyd’s, and for Aon to better serve its clients with capacity, the applicability of this tango-related metaphor is perhaps striking. Cortina could act as the market’s musical break, signalling a fundamental and maybe structural shift in who provides follow capacity and on what terms. Introducing a dynamic that may play out across the risk transfer ecosystem (much more broadly than within the Lloyd’s market alone) with ramifications for incumbents across reinsurance. Going back to the metaphor, in tango the Cortina is when the musical lead orchestrates the dance, cuing up a new rhythm or genre and structurally changing the flow of the evening. In reinsurance, the broker’s are increasingly orchestrating the flow of capital and how it gets matched with risk. By arranging a facility like Cortina, which has the ability to automatically write 3% of eligible property catastrophe excess-of-loss treaties and 5% of other eligible treaties arranged by Aon, the broker is actively curating the flow of premium to meet the needs of large capital providers. Aon is routing efficient, lower-friction institutional capital increasingly directly to the risk, bypassing the more traditional open-market syndication. If the Cortina strategy delivers for all parties, returning structural savings to cedants as a dividend-style discount to lead terms, delivering returns to the investors and importantly adding value for the brokers, then we can expect more of these structures to be cued up. Back to the metaphor. You could say that, the brokers are dictating the playlist and adjusting the rhythm of the reinsurance market, and alternative capital is increasingly their preferred track. Sticking with the tango, when the Cortina gets played it also signals a separation of the previous sets of partners. In follow-form facilities and broker facilities, traditional reinsurers and syndicates have often relied on the flow of premiums they deliver, as passive and often lucrative access to flow business can be a meaningful addition to their own underwriting efforts. With the use of the Lloyd’s infrastructure, alongside insurance-linked securities market plumbing in the form of the London Bridge 2 structure, initiatives like Cortina could bring in institutional and private credit-like asset management giants in the place of the more traditional capacity partner. Returning to the tango metaphor again, through Cortina, Blackstone can channel capital onto the dance floor without the operational friction, legacy liabilities, or high expense ratios associated with building a standalone reinsurance franchise. They are not there to debate the steps, they are there to execute their strategy (dance) algorithmically, strictly following the lead underwriter’s terms and claims decisions. This represents a further commoditisation of follow capacity by the ILS and alternative capital markets, although it also has broader ramifications outside pure follow-form strategies. When the Cortina plays in an Argentinian dancehall, it never signals the end of the night, but it does signal a changing, or mixing of the dance floor’s participants and fundamentally, sometimes structurally, resets the room. There are potentially significant implications of course, for those operating within Lloyd’s and perhaps beyond. The strategy has implications for anyone relying on follow-form access to premiums, especially syndicates that lack the specialist expertise to consistently lead complex placements in the underwriting market. Access to risk could be reduced, while the ability of the broker’s to reliably fill large amounts of a slip with efficient institutional capital could reduce some market participants pricing power and relevance. Those with the capability to price and lead on underwriting, while setting the terms and managing the claims in the process as well, may be able to command a premium, which does have the potential to bifurcate the market to a degree. Back to our tango metaphor, incumbents will need to be able to justify their expense ratios through top-tier underwriting talent and proprietary data, as those that are unable to lead the dance may struggle to secure their spot on the floor. Efficient following capacity at scale from players with potentially lower costs-of-capital also introduces a new pricing dynamic into the reinsurance market. Over-time, developments like this that become more widespread have the potential to compress pricing, make premium harder to come by and force incumbent reinsurers to compress their own margins to compete with the efficiency of institutional capital deployed through low-friction vehicles that borrow techniques from the insurance-linked securities market structure and form. Follow capacity, so-called ReShares and now increasingly we hear people in the market talking about indexing to meet large investors appetite. The broker that enables investors to access index-like returns more efficiently in reinsurance stands to gain a lot of power, which makes it a prize worth pursuing and this is starting to generate real attention it seems. It’s unclear at this stage whether Cortina is simply the latest remix of an old and established dance tune, or something more radical and heralding of real change, in the rhythm and flow of the reinsurance market. As broker’s own analytics, data, technology and pricing capabilities accelerate and become increasingly powerful in their own right, it does also raise questions over who is actually leading the dance these days and will be in future? Cortina syndicate 1956 sends yet another clear signal that the convergence of alternative, institutional capital and traditional reinsurance continues to evolve beyond the typical ILS structures we’ve seen for years and now occupies a growing role in the everyday flow of syndicated placements as well. For the traditional market, Cortina signals it. The music has changed and it’s time to learn the correct steps for a new rhythm that is being played. items.title: Nurse’s long COVID claim fails over lack of medical evidence
items.original_title: Nurse’s long COVID claim fails over lack of medical evidence
items.rss_title: Nurse’s long COVID claim fails over lack of medical evidence
items.rss_description: A New York hospital nurse who received workers compensation benefits after contracting COVID-19 at work failed to establish that her subsequent long COVID symptoms were related to the infection, an appeals court ruled Thursday.
items.extracted_text: Susan Hahnenfeld, a registered nurse at Good Samaritan Hospital, contracted COVID-19 in April 2020. A workers compensation law judge established her claim in 2022, authorized medical treatment and awarded lost-time benefits for approximately one month, according to Matter of Hahnenfeld v. Good Samaritan Hospital , filed in the state’s Appellate Division, Third Department. A judge later amended the claim to include long COVID, but the Workers’ Compensation Board reversed that decision in May 2025, citing insufficient evidence of causation. Ms. Hahnenfeld’s treating neurologist diagnosed her with long COVID after she reported leg pain, tremors, difficulty walking, fatigue and other symptoms. However, medical records also showed she had an autoimmune disorder, hypertension and cancer, and had contracted COVID-19 a second time in December 2021. Other physicians offered differing explanations for her symptoms, including inflammation and preexisting musculoskeletal conditions. Affirming the board’s decision, the appeals court found that the physicians’ testimony did not sufficiently establish a causal connection between her symptoms and the April 2020 workplace infection. The court also noted that long COVID symptoms may be compensable under an established COVID-19 claim without a separate amendment, provided the necessary causal relationship is demonstrated. items.extracted_text: Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners 12th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Through the recent period of brisk issuance the catastrophe bond market has been expanding rapidly, with now 20% more cat bond deals available to investors than a year ago, analysis from specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities investment manager Euler ILS Partners shows. In its review of the market after the third-quarter of 2026, Euler ILS Partners found that the size of the market had increased 17.3% year-on-year, while the number of deals outstanding rose slightly faster by 20% to reach 402. This expansion in market breadth means more individual investment opportunities are available to cat bond fund managers and investors, which helps in portfolio construction and diversification. But the metrics speak to a softening marketplace, with the average coupon of the cat bond market down 9.2% at 7.14% and the average spread down faster with a 21.6% decline YoY to 5.05%. The market has seen its issuance increasingly concentrated in the 1% to 3% expected loss range, Euler ILS Partners noted, which has raised the average expected loss of outstanding catastrophe bonds by 12.5% YoY to 2.4%. Euler ILS Partners’ data previously showed the average expected loss of the cat bond market had risen from 2.29% at the end of Q1 2026 to 2.31% by the end of the second-quarter , so the increase has continued. Euler ILS Partners commented as to how the market’s expected loss has developed, saying, “The share of issuance in the 1% to 3% expected-loss range increased from 37% in 2018 to 64% in 2026 YTD. As a result, lower-EL layers have become less prevalent in new issuance.” You can see how expected losses of catastrophe bond issuance have developed by year in the chart below, which shows the weighted average across 2026 issuance so far at 2.67%. Unweighted, Artemis’ data on catastrophe bond issuance expected losses shows the average at 2.85% in 2026 to-date, which is now the highest level since 2019 . Euler ILS Partners chart (above) shows issuance contracting fastest in the 1% to 2% EL range and increasing in the 2% to 3% range, which suggests the weighted average may increase further as this year progresses. Through reinsurance market cycles the average expected loss of cat bond issuance tends to rise when prices soften, as sponsors capitalise on being able to bring higher-risk deals to market. At the same time, through the third-quarter of 2026 the composition of perils in the cat bond market remained relatively stable according to Euler ILS Partners’ data. US hurricane risk still accounts for around 75% of exposure after Q3, so flat with the end of Q2 figure, but up from 74% as of the end of Q1. Euler ILS Partners said, “Cat Bond market composition remained broadly stable, with US hurricane risk represented in approximately 75% of exposure. items.original_title: National Beef Says Worst Is Over for US Cattle Cycle
items.rss_title: National Beef Says Worst Is Over for US Cattle Cycle
items.rss_description: Meatpacker National Beef Inc. said it is seeing a bottom in the US cattle industry’s downturn as it reported its highest margin in two years. “We do believe we are through the worst part of the cycle,” National Beef’s Chief …
items.extracted_text: National Beef Says Worst Is Over for US Cattle Cycle Article 0 Comments Meatpacker National Beef Inc. said it is seeing a bottom in the US cattle industry’s downturn as it reported its highest margin in two years. “We do believe we are through the worst part of the cycle,” National Beef’s Chief Executive Officer Tim Klein told journalists on Thursday. A reduction in overall slaughter in the US aided beef plant margins, while strong consumer demand kept beef prices elevated, he said. The Missouri-based beef producer controlled by Brazilian group MBRF Global Foods SA reported a margin of 2.1% considering earnings before items such as interest and taxes. That’s the highest since the third quarter of 2024. Cattle prices have surged as the US herd shrank to its smallest in decades due to droughts and high operating costs, tightening meatpackers’ margins. Recent earnings, however, have signaled at least some relief for the industry, with JBS NV on Monday also reporting improving results in its US beef unit. Beef supplies have become a key concern for the Trump administration, as prices for the protein remain an outsize driver of food inflation. It has encouraged more foreign ground beef imports and resumed live cattle shipments from Mexico, both moves that have helped meatpackers. MBRF’s results benefited from growing sales in the US and higher poultry exports even as Brazil faces restrictions in trade with Europe. A resumption in shipments is expected soon. Meanwhile, a recent outbreak of Newcastle disease hasn’t significantly affected poultry exports out of Brazil, the group’s CEO Miguel Gularte said. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. items.title: Trucking Company Settles Pregnancy Discrimination Lawsuit
items.original_title: Trucking Company Settles Pregnancy Discrimination Lawsuit
items.rss_title: Trucking Company Settles Pregnancy Discrimination Lawsuit
items.rss_description: Wabash National Corp., a nationwide producer of semi-trailers and other commercial trucking equipment and headquartered in Lafayette, Indiana, will pay $50,000 and provide other relief to settle a pregnancy discrimination lawsuit filed by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), …
items.extracted_text: Trucking Company Settles Pregnancy Discrimination Lawsuit Article 0 Comments Wabash National Corp., a nationwide producer of semi-trailers and other commercial trucking equipment and headquartered in Lafayette, Indiana, will pay $50,000 and provide other relief to settle a pregnancy discrimination lawsuit filed by the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), the agency announced. The EEOC’s suit charged that Wabash National’s facility in Cadiz, Kentucky denied a pregnant employee’s accommodation request to transfer to a role that did not require lying on her stomach. Instead, the company forced the employee to take unpaid leave and ultimately gave her no choice but to return to her position as an assembler without modification. Wabash National’s decision to deny the accommodation request caused the employee to fear for the health of her pregnancy, the EEOC said, and she was forced to resign at nearly eight months pregnant in November 2023. The company also unlawfully required the employee to provide medical documentation and failed to accommodate her even though it could have provided changes similar to those the company provides for non-pregnant workers with similar limitations, according to the suit. The alleged conduct violates the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, as amended, and the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, as amended (ADA). items.title: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic Hit With Lawsuit Seeking Halt to Frontier AI Development
items.original_title: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic Hit With Lawsuit Seeking Halt to Frontier AI Development
items.rss_title: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic Hit With Lawsuit Seeking Halt to Frontier AI Development
items.rss_description: A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology …
items.extracted_text: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic Hit With Lawsuit Seeking Halt to Frontier AI Development Article 0 Comments A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity. The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, about AI’s potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites. “No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the lawsuit says. “Nor is any industry granted the right to self-regulate the development of such dangerous products.” The lawsuit accuses the companies of engaging in business practices that create a public nuisance, or harm to public health and enjoyment, pointing to both past incidents and the potential for future harm. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Other Lawsuits Seek to Bar Development While the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation over fears it could harm the country’s ability to compete with China, states and private entities have sought to use lawsuits to force the companies to make changes. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, saying it has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. In September, Florida asked the judge overseeing the lawsuit to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending, according to court records. After Florida’s filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models and would not resume until they have additional safeguards in place. “Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company,” Pusateri said. Separately, a group of eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT has coached its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment after the filing. The states’ lawsuits seek financial penalties, as well as an order barring the company ⁠from developing self-improving AI models unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values. items.title: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive
items.original_title: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive
items.rss_title: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive
items.rss_description: In October, Shell Plc held a “DE&I in Action and World Mental Health” day, focused on inclusion and mental wellbeing. Staff in the U.S. and elsewhere were encouraged to reflect on their experiences at work, to “practice care, courage and …
items.extracted_text: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive Article 0 Comments In October, Shell Plc held a “DE&I in Action and World Mental Health” day, focused on inclusion and mental wellbeing. Staff in the U.S. and elsewhere were encouraged to reflect on their experiences at work, to “practice care, courage and curiosity” and to use a special video-conference background to mark the occasion. For an oil major that does business with the U.S. government, the mere existence of the event is notable. At a time when many global companies are downplaying diversity measures, London-headquartered Shell — which counts the U.S. as its biggest country market — is vocal in its commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion, calling it “a key driver for our winning performance culture.” That stance helps Shell comply with global diversity regulations that are non-negotiable for businesses based outside of the U.S. But it also increases the risk of scrutiny from the Trump administration and conservative activists. Shell’s DEI commitment has become central to legal challenges filed by three current or former employees represented by an activist group co-founded by President Donald Trump’s new Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller. The workers claim to have been discriminated against because they are White, describing a team restructure that favored ethnic-minority colleagues and foreign nationals, as well as a manager who they say gave them “tear jars” as jokey leaving gifts, which they found insensitive. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — whose Trump-appointed chair has urged White men to report workplace discrimination — did not take up the case but gave the trio notice of the right to sue, an administrative step. In March, a judge will review whether one of the cases is ready to proceed to trial, according to court filings. Stephen Miller Photographer: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg Shell strongly rebuts the allegations, a company spokesperson said, adding that it does not tolerate discrimination and makes employment decisions based on merit and business needs. The business complies with local laws and regulations in countries where it operates, the spokesperson added. Shell also said in a legal filing that the unit the plaintiffs worked for has a long-standing practice of giving departing employees iconic blue-and-white Dutch pottery in recognition of their time at the company. Employment discrimination lawsuits don’t typically threaten large corporations’ core operations or business viability. And people with knowledge of the oil and gas sector said that firms like Shell broadly have good relationships with the Trump administration and more pressing concerns than DEI. Nonetheless, these cases can cause reputational damage, incur legal costs and soak up managers’ time and attention. They also show how Trump’s DEI pushback is being pursued. “We’re seeing more enforcement activity where we hadn’t seen enforcement activity before,” said Samia Kirmani, a Boston-based attorney at Jackson Lewis PC, which focuses on employment law. The EEOC has already stepped up its pursuit of DEI-related cases through policy statements and guidance notified Fortune 500 companies that it’s prepared to litigate over DEI filed a lawsuit against a Coca-Cola Co. distributor over a women’s-only retreat and this month settled with Lockheed Martin Corp. over alleged discrimination against White employees related to performance and compensation decisions. While the Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterm elections this month has altered the political landscape, the implications for government actions on DEI remain to be seen. Of the 32 workplace DEI-discrimination lawsuits ongoing across the country right now, most concern White people claiming discrimination, according to New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging. In addition to the EEOC’s growing appetite for enforcement, there are President Trump’s own executive orders and directives from the Department of Justice to consider, Kirmani said, meaning businesses across the board can’t ignore the prospect of future legal action. Scaling Back In the American workforce, White people hold about 80% of all management roles and have one of the lowest unemployment rates of any cohort. The Trump administration has prioritized fighting what it describes as racism against White workers, barring federal contractors from engaging in “illegal DEI.” In response, companies like McDonald’s Corp. and Ford Motor Co. have scaled back their inclusion efforts. Meanwhile, Shell, which is among the world’s largest energy companies and is enjoying healthy financial growth after several years of cost-cutting, has continued to set measurable global diversity targets, although it does not target specific numbers in the U.S. It aims for women to hold 40% of global senior leadership positions by 2030. It maintains a Global Council for Race — a group of senior Shell leaders aiming to advance workforce diversity, who do not make individual employment decisions — and supports employee groups focused on race and ethnicity, as well as LGBTQ+ and disability inclusion. In the U.K. and European Union, where diversity rules mainly focus on gender rather than race, companies are required to meet targets and follow disclosure rules around things like board diversity, gender pay gaps and pay transparency. Countries including Japan and Australia also impose diversity regulations on corporations. To operate in these jurisdictions, U.S. companies must meet these requirements too, regardless of their approach at home. Thomas Hutt holds the tear jar he says was given to him by his former boss at Shell. Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg Measures like holding DEI events aren’t specifically covered by these regulations. But the oil and gas industry often struggles to bring in women and needs to maintain a balanced global workforce to do business in many countries, said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at New York University who focuses on corporate responsibility and business ethics. “They tend to operate via moving people around,” she said. In lawsuits filed in Texas, the most recent of them in August, three people who work or have worked in Shell’s U.S. corporate security unit allege that the company violated employment laws. They are seeking back pay, compensation for future lost earnings, benefits and damages from Shell, without specifying a figure. The plaintiffs allege that the oil company favored minority workers at their expense during a restructuring of their division in January 2025 — just as Trump was beginning his second term and when many companies were already scaling back their DEI efforts. Miller’s America First Legal, which lists dismantling DEI as a priority on its website, is also representing White people in cases against corporations including TV network CBS, Meta Platforms Inc. and International Business Machines Corp. “Federal civil rights laws protect every American, and America First Legal is fighting to hold Shell accountable for violating those protections in the name of ‘DEI,'” AFL spokeswoman Alexa Vance said in an emailed statement. “Shell touts its commitment to ‘diversity’ while simultaneously showing high-performing, longtime employees the door because they are White.” Complaints like those against Shell are victories for right-wing groups because they support their broader media campaign and narrative, said Jonathan Feingold, a law professor at Boston University. “Large corporations often have actually pretty shallow commitments to reckon with the way in which misogyny or racism manifest in their institutions,” he said. In his complaint, Thomas Hutt, a former manager in Shell’s corporate security unit, said he was forced to reapply for his role after almost 15 years at the company, during which he received strong performance reviews. Hutt said his manager Wayne Hunt, a defendant in the case, had said he was looking to “diversify the talent.” Hutt said he was ultimately replaced by a Black colleague who, in his view, lacked experience in corporate security, having previously worked in fraud investigations. When he left the job, Hutt said that Hunt gave him a “tear jar” — a small, decorative vessel, supposedly for collecting tears — to mock him. Two of Hutt’s colleagues, Kevin Taylor and Michelle Romak, jointly filed a similar complaint in August last year. They said they were told to reapply for their roles during the 2025 reorganization, while minority employees weren’t. They allege that some minority applicants for jobs within the team got preferential treatment, such as interview coaching. In a formal written response to the allegations dated Oct. 16, 2025, Shell said that a coaching session was to help an employee join its corporate security group, not to prepare them for interviews. Taylor, who still works at Shell, said in the complaint that he was demoted and forced to transfer from company headquarters to another state, while a Hispanic contractor, who Taylor said was under-performing, was given his preferred role. In its response, Shell denied the allegations but accepted that Hunt had approved Taylor’s transfer. Romak was ultimately laid off and said Hunt also gave her a tear jar. The EEOC declined to comment, while the White House didn’t respond to emails seeking comment. Polarized Views During an internal company webcast around the time of Trump’s January 2025 inauguration, Shell Chief Legal Officer Philippa Bounds was asked how Trump’s policies may affect its contracts and said the company was not turning its back on DEI, according to a former employee who declined to be identified discussing internal communications. Shell did not comment on the matter. On employee-review website Glassdoor, Shell ranks 4.1 out of 5 for its DE&I measures. Some employees have also praised the company’s efforts on platforms like LinkedIn, where one employee wrote earlier this year that she was proud to work with “everyone who makes diversity, equity and inclusion real.” But for some former employees in the U.S., Shell’s approach has been a frustration. One ex-supervisor who worked offshore said he believed staff reductions disproportionately affected White, male workers and that he was compelled to give presentations on LGBTQ issues that he felt conflicted with his Christian faith. The supervisor declined to be identified, citing a non-disclosure agreement. Another former offshore worker, who also asked not to be named, said he believed Shell aimed to make its Whale production platform the most diverse in the Gulf of Mexico and that managers actively sought Black and other minority employees for leadership-development programs. In his view, DEI impacted morale among White, male employees who felt overlooked and unable to voice criticism. As Americans’ perspectives on DEI have become more polarized, the workload for international companies has only increased. “Whenever the wind blows one way, we have one kind of lawsuit, and then when the wind blows the other way, we have another kind of lawsuit,” said Katie Mehnert, who is chief executive officer of Houston-based workforce development company Ally Energy and has also worked at Shell. “It’s just a very disruptive approach to how to do business.” Top photo: Thomas Hutt Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg.
